questions.q: Why can't Azure Cognitive Services' prebuilt models be abstracted behind a thin interface the way a message queue can?
options: Amazon's adjacent services (Textract, Rekognition) solve similar problems with genuinely different APIs, accuracy characteristics, and configuration models, so there is no comparable capability to abstract toward
Cognitive Services does not have a REST API
AWS does not allow calling any AI services from Terraform
Cognitive Services can only be called from inside Azure Kubernetes Service
questions.explain: Unlike a queue or a basic database, there is no AWS service with the same feature granularity as a given Cognitive Services capability — the AWS alternatives differ enough that any 'abstraction' would really be two separate, differently-behaved integrations.

questions.q: What makes AWS Step Functions and Azure Logic Apps a poor fit for the adapter pattern from Lesson 10?
options: Neither service can be provisioned with Terraform
They are both deprecated in favor of Kubernetes-native workflow engines
Only one of the two actually orchestrates multi-step workflows
Their state-machine definition languages, retry semantics, and connector catalogs are not interchangeable, so a workflow built against one requires a rewrite, not a config change, to run on the other
questions.explain: Both services orchestrate workflows, but the underlying definition languages and behaviors differ enough that porting a workflow between them is a genuine rewrite, unlike swapping a thin queue adapter.

questions.q: According to the lesson's gut-check question, when should you NOT build a portability layer for a specific service integration?
options: When the service is a basic relational database
When you would actually tolerate rewriting that one integration if you ever switched clouds, since the one-time rewrite cost is smaller than the recurring cost of maintaining an abstraction today
When the service runs inside a Kubernetes cluster
When more than one engineer on the team disagrees about cloud strategy
questions.explain: The lesson's gut check is: if you'd honestly tolerate a future rewrite of that specific piece, building and maintaining an abstraction layer for it now costs more than the optionality is worth.

questions.q: Under the 'portability budget' framing, where should multi-cloud abstraction effort actually be spent?
options: Equally across every single cloud service a system uses, with no exceptions
Only on logging and monitoring dashboards
On the core application workload and commodity services with real equivalents everywhere (object storage, a relational database, a basic message queue) — not on deep, differentiated platform services
Nowhere — multi-cloud abstraction is never worth building
questions.explain: The lesson recommends spending portability effort where there's a real choice and a real equivalent (the workload itself, commodity services), and skipping it for deep platform integrations with no honest equivalent to abstract toward.

questions.q: Why is building an abstraction layer around DynamoDB's global-table behavior, aimed at Cosmos DB, described as risky in this lesson?
options: DynamoDB cannot be provisioned through Terraform

Cosmos DB's consistency levels, pricing model, and partition-key behavior differ enough that code tuned against one will not perform or cost the same against the other, so the abstraction wouldn't actually deliver equivalent behavior
Cosmos DB does not support global distribution at all
DynamoDB and Cosmos DB use the exact same API, so no abstraction is needed in the first place
questions.explain: Cosmos DB is a comparably capable globally distributed database, but its consistency model, request-unit pricing, and partition-key behavior are different enough that an abstraction can't guarantee equivalent performance or cost across the two.
